analysis.one_liner: Forces health plans to prove and disclose they cover mental health care equally, with audits and a consumer complaint line.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a House floor vote: after a single subcommittee hearing in June 2020, it sat in committee until the Congress ended, despite 26 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already says insurance plans must cover mental health and substance use care no less generously than physical care, but enforcement is weak and restrictions are hard for patients to see. This bill would require plans and insurers to publish, every year, the analyses showing how they comply — especially the murky, non-numerical restrictions like prior-authorization rules — and would let federal agencies audit at least 12 plans a year. It would also create a consumer unit with a toll-free hotline and website so people denied care can file complaints and get answers, and it would make agencies track how often mental health claims are denied compared with other claims.
analysis.who_benefits: People with mental health or substance use disorder coverage under group or individual plans — tens of millions of Americans — especially those whose claims or treatment limits have been quietly restricted in ways the parity law forbids. Consumers would finally see the plan's own compliance analysis, get a single hotline and web portal for complaints, and receive written responses about what happened to their complaint. Treatment providers also benefit indirectly when patients' claims are actually paid.

how_it_helps.text: Plans and insurers would have to file an annual public report detailing exactly how they apply non-numerical treatment restrictions — like prior authorization and medical-necessity standards — to mental health and substance use benefits versus medical and surgical benefits, and disclose the plan documents, formulas, and methodologies used to set benefits.

HHS, Labor, and the Treasury would have to conduct randomized audits of at least 12 plans or coverages per year, plus on-demand audits of any plan's books and records, and post de-identified audit results on a public website.

A new consumer parity unit at HHS would run a single toll-free number and public web portal for parity complaints, give consumers a clear process and timeline for filing them, and require plans to respond and agencies to report back on enforcement steps taken.

Federal agencies would collect and report to Congress the rates of, and reasons for, denials of mental health and substance use claims compared with medical and surgical claims — data that does not systematically exist today.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group health plans bear the cost: annual compliance analyses, new disclosures, audit exposure, and formal complaint-response obligations. If enforcement forces plans to actually cover more mental health care, some of that cost could show up in premiums or employer benefit spending — which is the point of the law being enforced.

drawbacks.text: The disclosure, audit, and complaint-response requirements impose real administrative costs on insurers and employer plans, and strict parity enforcement could raise premiums or employer benefit costs if plans must cover services they currently restrict.

The bill is largely a transparency and enforcement bill, not a coverage mandate: it makes plans prove and publish compliance but writes no new funding or staffing levels for the consumer unit or the audits, so its practical power depends entirely on how aggressively agencies implement it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is concrete for a population that is routinely denied care on technicalities they cannot see: published parity analyses, audit results, and denial-rate data would give patients, regulators, and Congress the evidence the current law lacks, and a single hotline would replace a maze of unclear complaint channels. The costs are real but ordinary for insurance regulation — paperwork, audit exposure, and possibly somewhat higher premiums where plans have been under-covering mental health. On balance, a well-designed transparency and enforcement measure whose main cost falls on parties already legally required to comply.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees for a year and a half, got exactly one subcommittee hearing, and was never brought to a committee vote or the House floor before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy III introduced the bill on May 21, 2019, joined by 12 original cosponsors.
It was referred to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — splitting jurisdiction and making advancement harder.
Eight days after introduction it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed.
The subcommittee held a hearing on June 30, 2020 — the only recorded action in the bill's 19-month life.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer group health plans are better off: they never had to publish their parity compliance analyses, submit to audits, or operate under a centralized complaint system, so the restrictions the parity law was supposed to prevent remain as opaque as before.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the House's 197 Republicans signed on; since the bill never reached a vote, no recorded party split exists beyond the cosponsor list.

industries.note: Insurers would have to publish annual analyses showing how they restrict mental health care, submit to federal audits of at least 12 plans a year, and report claim denial rates — exposing and deterring the hidden restrictions that let them pay out less on mental health claims than the law allows. Their interest in avoiding this scrutiny runs directly against patients' interest in having claims honored.

Employer plans face the same disclosure, audit, and complaint-response duties, adding compliance cost. Most already fall short of the parity law they would be forced to demonstrate compliance with, so their cost savings from under-covering mental health are what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Mental health and addiction treatment providers
industries.note: Stronger parity enforcement means insurers deny fewer behavioral health claims and reimburse more care, so providers get paid and patients can actually use their benefits. Their gain runs alongside patients'.
